newsitem.title: HONG KONG: South Korea borrowers to gain from OECD membership.
newsitem.headline: South Korea borrowers to gain from OECD membership.

text.p: South Korean borrowers may be able to pay a bit less for funding now that the country has been invited to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, traders and analysts said on Monday.

"For a lot of the Korean banks, getting into the OECD is a big benefit because many investors abide by BIS (Bank for International Settlements) rules and were hesitant about taking Korean paper before," said a trader at a Japanese bank.

Under BIS guidelines, loans to OECD member country banks qualify for a 20 percent rather than 100 percent risk weighting. The lower risk weighting effectively increases the return to lenders holding OECD paper.

"People are quite willing to accept lower spreads if they know that their return on capital is going to be five times greater when Korea becomes an OECD member," said a bank syndicate manager in Hong Kong.
If the OECD's offer is accepted, South Korea will become the 29th country, and the second Asian nation after Japan, to join.

Spreads on South Korean commercial banks' floating rate notes have tightened a few basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, in the secondary market since the OECD announced its invitation late Friday, traders said.

Hanil Bank's notes due in 1999 were offered at 25 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate and bid at 27 basis points, two to three basis points tighter than on Friday morning. Other A3-rated bank notes tightened by similar amounts.
Most of the movement in bank spreads occurred before last Friday because bankers have been betting for some time that South Korea would join the OECD before year's end.
Some bankers in Hong Kong said that Korean bank spreads have already come in enough and that further tightening could discourage traditional lenders from taking on more paper.
But they acknowledged that OECD membership could attract new lenders, particularly from Europe.
Korean banks may also find it easier to extend tenors beyond the three years that has been the norm lately, they said.

The change in South Korea's risk weighting does not offer any benefit to institutional investors, but bankers said OECD membership and a generally brighter outlook for the country means that bonds of South Korean borrowers remain a buy.
Bonds of Korean quasi-sovereign borrowers still pay a higher return than similarly rated sovereign issues of other countries.

In February, Canada's province of Ontario, which is rated Aa3 by Moody's Investors Service and AA-minus by Standard and Poor's Corp, launched a 10-year global bond that was priced to yield 48 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
In contrast, quasi-sovereign Korea Development Bank's 10-year global bond priced at 74 basis points over Treasuries when it was launched in May.

The KDB bond's price has appreciated so much since launch that its spread to Treasuries is now in the "low to to mid-fifties", said Glenn Kim, senior vice president at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong. Ontario's bond is in the low to mid-40s.
"If you had bought into Korea as one of your principal investments, you clearly would have made a fortune from a relative value perspective," he said.

Investors that take on quasi-sovereign paper now probably can't hope for the same type of gains, but they could still pick up several basis points, especially if Moody's raises Korea, as is widely expected.
Ontario and Korean are ranked the same by S&P at AA-minus, but Korea is tagged with a lower A1 rating from Moody's.
"I'm optimistic that we will see more spread compression with a Moody's move," said Kim.

"We may also find that there are incremental investors that see OECD membership and Korea's good fundamentals as good reasons to get into the market with the view to an upgrade in the near future," he said.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843-6371
